sources.life: In his 1948 Tennessee Senate race, Memphis boss E. H. Crump's side likened him to a raccoon. Kefauver answered in a coonskin cap, saying he might be a pet coon but not Crump's, won, and kept the cap as his trademark.

patterns.moment: {boss} calls you a name meant to stick, and {staffer} hands you a way to wear it.
choices: answer with a line that turns it around
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer, and the name belongs to {rival}'s side.

patterns.title: Your past comes out

roles.fill: a membership or act from years back on your record

setting.text: Where the press would find you that day.

gates: Candidate.
{the old act} is on your record and a rival can find it.

branches.then: A letter in your own hand shows more than you said. A denial now is a caught lie.

branches.when: you call it the worst mistake of your life
branches.then: The line goes on your record and follows you.

sources.life: In his first House race in West Virginia in 1952, a primary opponent revealed his past Ku Klux Klan membership. Byrd said he had joined in the early 1940s and left; his Republican opponent later found a 1946 letter from Byrd to the Klan's leader. He won, and years later called joining the worst mistake of his life.

patterns.moment: {rival} tells the press about {the old act}.
choices: own it and say why you left
play it down (a lie if the record says more)
go on the air about it
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you did not answer, and the story runs its course.

patterns.title: Your own words, cut up

roles.fill: books, columns, posts or old speeches on your record

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
A body of writing or speeches on your record.

branches.then: A big employer docks pay or presses staff to give to {rival}, and a worker tells you.
Filmed voter interviews against you turn out to use actors, and exposing it is a press story.

sources.life: Running for California governor in 1934, he was hit with out-of-context quotes from his own novels run daily in the papers, and with newsreels of staged voter interviews; studio heads pressured employees to give to his opponent. He lost.

patterns.moment: {rival}'s side runs lines from {your writing}, cut from their context, every day.
choices: say the words were a character's, not yours
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer, and the quotes become what people think you said.

patterns.title: The attack on your partner

roles.fill: a paper or station on record
your partner

setting.text: Where you would answer: the outlet's door, a statement, your own front steps.

gates: Candidate.
An attack on {household member} on the press record.

branches.then: The press says you cried, or that it was melting snow, and the story becomes your composure.

branches.when: the letter behind it was forged
branches.then: Later it comes out that a rival campaign planted it. The lie is theirs on the record.

branches.when: you win by less than expected
branches.then: The margin reads as a loss.

sources.life: Two weeks before the 1972 New Hampshire primary, the Manchester Union Leader ran a letter accusing him of laughing at a slur and an editorial attacking his wife. He answered outside the paper's offices in the snow, and reporters wrote that he cried, which he denied. The letter was later tied to the Nixon campaign's dirty tricks.

patterns.moment: {outlet} has attacked {household member} in print, days before the vote.
choices: answer it in public, at the outlet's door
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let it stand.

patterns.title: The letter in the last week

roles.fill: your faith, your marriage, or a false charge against you

setting.text: Wherever it reaches you.

gates: Candidate, in the final week.
A letter or flyer on record.

branches.then: {rival} disowns it or does not, and both are records.
Answering gives it air; not answering lets it spread.

sources.life: Late in his 1990 race, a letter from his opponent's supporters attacked him for marrying a non-Jew, and Wellstone fired back.
In the 1983 Chicago race a flier made a false criminal accusation against him.

patterns.moment: In the final week, a letter or flyer goes around about {the target}.
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer.

patterns.title: Your name is the only reason

roles.fill: a well-known officeholder in your family

setting.text: the debate stage, because the line is said in front of everyone.

gates: Candidate in a debate.
{your relative} is on your record.

branches.then: Your aide steers you out of the hall before you do anything.
People who listened think {rival} won; people who watched think you did.

branches.when: the line makes you the underdog
branches.then: A supporter says {rival} made a rich candidate the underdog.

sources.life: In a South Boston debate for the 1962 Massachusetts Senate primary, Edward McCormack said Kennedy's candidacy would be a joke if his name were Edward Moore. Kennedy's voice reportedly shook in his closing, an aide steered him out afterward, and he won the primary by more than two to one.

patterns.moment: On the debate stage, {rival} says that without your family's name your run would be a joke.
choices: answer with what you have done yourself
let it pass and give your closing
hit back at {rival}'s own family ties
lose your temper (only with the traits for it)
patterns.ifNo: Letting it pass writes that you took it. How it reads depends on who watched and who listened.

patterns.title: Who gets on the stage

roles.fill: the moderator, said with the outlet that set up the debate

setting.text: the debate hall, because the stage is what is being fought over.

gates: Candidate.
A debate on the calendar that your campaign paid for.
weights: How far ahead or behind you are.

branches.when: you are the one left out
branches.then: You stand at the edge of the stage, and leaving quietly or speaking up is the scene.

branches.when: {rival} refuses to go on with the others
branches.then: {rival} looks small or principled, by the room.

sources.life: Before the 1980 New Hampshire primary he paid for a debate a Nashua paper set up with George H. W. Bush and invited the other candidates. Bush refused to debate with them, the moderator ordered Reagan's microphone cut, and Reagan said he was paying for it. He won the primary easily.

patterns.moment: You paid for the debate and brought the other candidates, and {moderator} orders your microphone cut.
choices: insist you are paying for it
go along with the two-person format
walk off with the candidates who were left out
patterns.ifNo: Going along writes that you took the sponsor's format, and the left-out candidates remember.

patterns.title: The comparison

roles.fill: a revered officeholder from the world's own history
an opponent on record with a tie to {the figure}

setting.text: the debate stage.

gates: Candidate in a debate.
{the figure} is in the world's history, and {rival}'s tie to them is on record.

branches.then: The warning is on record, and making it anyway is your choice.

branches.when: you are the one who knew them
branches.then: Deliver the rebuke, or let it go.

branches.when: you lose the exchange and win the race
branches.then: The line follows you anyway.

sources.life: Pressed on experience in the 1988 vice-presidential debate, Quayle compared his time in Congress to John F. Kennedy's. Bentsen, who had known Kennedy, told him he was no Jack Kennedy. Quayle's advisers had warned him, and the ticket won anyway.

patterns.moment: You might compare yourself on stage to {the figure}, and {rival} knew them.
choices: prepare an answer in case it comes up
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it out writes nothing.

patterns.title: Under the lights

roles.fill: whoever handles the broadcast

setting.text: Where you get ready before the broadcast.

gates: Candidate.
A televised debate on the calendar.
weights: How tired you are on the record.

branches.then: You look pale under the lights, and people talk about how you looked more than what you said.
They look fresh, and the comparison is made for you.
The papers argue for weeks about whether it mattered.

sources.person: John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon
sources.life: Before the first televised debate in 1960, Nixon had been ill and hurt his knee and looked pale in a gray suit that blended into the set; accounts differ on his makeup. Kennedy had practiced and rested. The claim that radio listeners judged it differently rests on thin polling.

patterns.moment: The first televised debate is tonight, and {staffer} asks how you want to look.
choices: change your clothes for the set
patterns.ifNo: Going on as you are writes nothing. The camera decides.

patterns.title: The first spots

roles.fill: an advertising man or consultant

setting.text: Where the spots are filmed: a studio, an office made up for it.

gates: Candidate.
An ad budget on the reports.

branches.when: the voters are recruited off the street
branches.then: They are filmed apart from you, looking up as if at you, and a reporter can find out.
Their reach falls behind yours.

sources.life: In 1952 adman Rosser Reeves persuaded him that short spots placed near shows like I Love Lucy would reach more people than long speeches. Eisenhower read answers from cue cards to questions from tourists filmed separately. Adlai Stevenson refused to appear in his own TV ads.

patterns.moment: {ad maker} wants you to read short answers to ordinary voters' questions, filmed apart from them, to run between popular shows.
choices: do them only with real voters in the room
patterns.ifNo: Refusing writes that you would not be sold like soap, and {rival}'s spots run.

patterns.title: The line on every sign

roles.fill: whoever runs your message

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
weights: How well the line fits your record.

branches.when: the line plays on who you are
branches.then: It works where people already see you that way and costs you where they do not.
A hat, a color or a cap becomes yours.
The line becomes a target.

sources.life: Running against a 14-year incumbent in a 1970 Manhattan Democratic primary, she used the slogan that a woman's place is in the House, the House of Representatives, was known for her hats, and won.

patterns.moment: {staffer} wants one line for every sign and ad, and the pick is yours.
choices: a line built from your own record and who you are (four drawn from it)
patterns.ifNo: Just your name writes a plain campaign. Doors and ads carry no message.

patterns.title: Nobody sent you

roles.fill: the party's ward or district office
the party's man for the ward, said with the post

setting.text: {the party office}, because the door is the moment.

gates: Not in office.
{the party office} is on record in your area.
weights: Your ties to anyone in the party.
How closed the local party is.

branches.then: The name opens the door, and you owe the name.

branches.when: you go to the reform side
branches.then: The faction tie is the start of your career.

sources.life: In 1948 he walked into his Chicago ward office to volunteer for Adlai Stevenson and Paul Douglas. Asked who sent him, he said nobody, and was turned away; he later called it the start of his political career.

patterns.moment: You offer to volunteer at {the party office}, and {committeeman} asks who sent you.
choices: leave and find another way in: a reform club, an independent group
come back with someone who vouches for you
patterns.ifNo: Leaving writes that the party turned you away. Another group may find you.

patterns.title: Register them first

roles.fill: someone who runs house meetings and registration drives

setting.text: Where {organizer} would find you: after a meeting they ran, at your door.

gates: Adults who are not registered live in a part of your district that would back you, by the voter roll.

branches.then: The drive is your answer to the loss.
The groups that join expect their share after the win.

sources.life: After he lost a Los Angeles council race in 1947, the Community Service Organization he helped found, with organizer Fred Ross holding house meetings, registered about 15,000 new voters in Boyle Heights. With labor and Jewish voters behind him, he won in 1949.

patterns.moment: {organizer} says the people who would vote for you are not registered, and asks for months before you run.
choices: spend months registering voters before you run
run now with who is registered
join with labor and other groups to share the work
patterns.ifNo: Running now writes that you ran on the rolls as they were.

patterns.title: Go where people already are

roles.fill: whoever runs your schedule

setting.text: Wherever the campaign plans its week.

gates: Candidate.
The district's places are on record.
weights: How spread out the district is.
Ties from a cause you worked for.

branches.then: People you worked with before turn out and host you.
The family's ties set the stops.

sources.life: Running statewide in Montana in 1916, she spoke at train stations, street corners, potlucks and one-room schools, drawing on the network from her suffrage campaigns, and became the first woman elected to Congress.

patterns.moment: Your district is wide and thinly settled, and {staffer} asks where next week's stops go.
choices: where crowds already gather: the station, a supper, a school event
where your network from an earlier cause lives
patterns.ifNo: Staying in the towns writes that the far places never saw you.

patterns.title: The volunteer who wants a real job

roles.fill: a volunteer on record with weeks of work

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
{volunteer}'s work is on record.

branches.when: many of your volunteers are parents
branches.then: Child care at the office changes who can come.
They come back to ask for your endorsement.

sources.life: Her 1970 campaign office offered free drop-in child care, and she pushed to promote women from canvassers into staff jobs.

patterns.moment: {volunteer}, who has knocked doors for weeks, asks for a staff job over a hired professional.
choices: set up child care at the office so parents can volunteer
patterns.ifNo: Keeping roles writes that you kept them a volunteer, and they may drift away.

patterns.title: Follow me around

roles.fill: a reporter, said with the outlet
something in your household record a reporter could learn

setting.text: Where {reporter} would confront you: outside your home, by your car.

gates: Candidate.
{the private fact} is on your record and a reporter could learn it.
weights: Whether you dared reporters to follow you.

branches.when: you told reporters to follow you
branches.then: They did, and the remark is quoted back.
Months later you return, and the first question is the old one.

sources.life: In 1987 he told a reporter that anyone who wanted could follow him around. The Miami Herald acted on a tip, watched his townhouse and confronted him, and he suspended his campaign within days.

patterns.moment: {reporter} asks about {the private fact} after a tip, and says they watched your home.
patterns.ifNo: Refusing writes that you would not answer, and the story runs without you.

patterns.title: A line of your own

roles.fill: whoever runs your effort

setting.text: Wherever the effort meets.

gates: Candidate not nominated by a major party.
weights: How unpopular the major parties are on record.
How many candidates split the vote.

branches.when: the state will not list your party
branches.then: You sue to get it listed.
You win with a plurality, and the record says how few chose you.

branches.when: reformers of both parties back a fusion ticket
branches.then: Each expects its share after the win.

sources.life: A Socialist Alternative candidate, she sued the state to list her party on the 2012 ballot, lost that race, and in 2013 beat a long-serving Seattle council member on a $15 minimum wage platform.
He ran for New York mayor in 1933 on a Fusion ticket backed by reformers, Republicans and anti-Tammany Democrats, and won.
He left the Republicans and won the 1990 Connecticut governor's race on his own A Connecticut Party line with about 40 percent in a three-way race.

patterns.moment: Neither big party will nominate you, and {organizer} asks how you get on the ballot.
choices: run on a small party's line, suing if it is kept off
run on a fusion line with reformers of both parties
patterns.ifNo: Staying out writes that you did not run. Your backers find someone else.

patterns.title: Ahead at eleven

roles.fill: your manager, with the count

setting.text: Where you watch the returns: headquarters, a hotel, home.

gates: Election night.
Ballots still out on the count record: absentees, late counties.

branches.then: The claim is on record, the press replays it, and conceding weeks later reads worse.
Concede now or wait; the late ballots may be yours.

branches.when: the morning paper names the wrong winner
branches.then: An early edition called it for the loser, and holding it up is the morning's picture.

sources.life: In California's 2010 attorney general race, Republican Cooley declared victory on election night. Ballots counted afterward flipped the race, the lead swung for about three weeks, and he conceded to Harris.
Some outlets projected him the winner of California's 1982 governor's race early in the night; once absentee ballots were counted he lost narrowly.
In 1948 an early edition of the Chicago Daily Tribune declared him the winner, and Harry Truman held up a copy for photographers.

patterns.moment: Early returns have you or {rival} ahead, and {campaign manager} says many ballots are still out.
choices: say every ballot counts and wait
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes no claim, so there is nothing to take back.

patterns.title: The tie

roles.fill: the election official who runs the drawing

setting.text: wherever the law holds the drawing, because the draw is the moment.

gates: A tie on the count record.
The state's or place's tie law.
weights: What rides on the seat, such as control of the body.

branches.then: The recount puts you ahead by one; a court then counts a disputed ballot and it is tied.

branches.when: control of the body rides on it
branches.then: The leaders of both parties call you.
{clerk} picks the game of chance, beads, dice or a coin, and both sides must accept it.
The official canvass after a coin toss shows one side ahead, and the toss means nothing.

sources.life: A 2017 recount for a Virginia House seat put Democrat Simonds ahead by one vote. A court panel then counted a disputed ballot for Republican Yancey, making a tie; his name was drawn from a bowl, keeping a Republican majority.
A tied 2024 Corpus Christi council runoff was settled in 2025 by drawing numbered beads, after a roll of a die set the order.
A tied 2018 council race was settled by a coin toss; the official canvass then showed the incumbent ahead.

patterns.moment: After the recount and the court, the race is tied, and the law says the winner is drawn by lot.
choices: challenge the disputed ballot in court
patterns.ifNo: Conceding before the draw writes that you gave up the seat.

patterns.title: The long count

roles.fill: your lawyer

setting.text: Where you hear the count: headquarters, a call from {lawyer}.

gates: A margin inside the recount rule on the count record.

branches.then: Months late, colleagues walk you in, and the oath is done twice so your family can stand with you.
A concession after months reads differently from one on the night.

sources.life: Minnesota's 2008 Senate race went through a recount and a court contest for eight months. The state supreme court ruled for Franken by 312 votes, Coleman conceded, and Franken was sworn in that July, escorted by Amy Klobuchar and Walter Mondale.

patterns.moment: The margin is a few hundred votes, the recount and the court fight will take months, and the seat sits empty.
patterns.ifNo: Conceding writes it, and {rival} is sworn in.

patterns.title: Write me in

roles.fill: your closest adviser

setting.text: Where you take the news of the primary loss.

gates: You lost your party's primary.
The state allows write-ins.
weights: How well known your name is.

branches.then: The campaign's doors and ads are about how to write your name.
{rival}'s observers challenge each misspelled ballot, and the election official decides which count.
You are the first in years to win this way, and the party that dropped you has to deal with you.

sources.life: After losing Alaska's 2010 Republican primary to Joe Miller, she ran as a write-in, taught voters to spell her name, and won. At the hand count Miller's observers challenged ballots over spelling, even a cursive letter, and the elections director made the calls.

patterns.moment: You lost the primary, and {staffer} asks whether you run anyway as a write-in.
patterns.ifNo: Conceding writes it, and the nominee expects your endorsement.

patterns.title: The concession call

roles.fill: the candidate who won
your campaign chair, who can speak for you

setting.text: Where you watch the returns, with the people who worked for you.

gates: Election night.
The count record shows you behind.

branches.when: the margin collapses after you called
branches.then: You call back and take it back, after the other side has begun to celebrate.

branches.when: you call in private and speak in the morning
branches.then: The crowd goes home without you, and the next day's speech is the concession on record.

branches.when: you are the winner taking the call
branches.then: Take the concession graciously, or snap when it is taken back.

sources.life: On election night 2000, after the networks called Florida for George W. Bush, Gore phoned Bush to concede, then, as the margin shrank, called back to take it back. His campaign chairman told the crowd the race was too close to call.
In 2016 her campaign chairman told the crowd to go home; she called the winner that night and gave her concession speech the next morning.

patterns.moment: The count says you lost, and {campaign manager} holds the phone: call {winner} now, later, or not yet.
choices: call to concede now (the call follows its real form)
send {chairman} to tell the crowd to go home
speak to the crowd yourself tonight
patterns.ifNo: Not calling writes no concession, and the press asks why.

patterns.title: The crowd boos the winner

roles.fill: the candidate who beat you

setting.text: Where your supporters gathered for the night.

gates: You conceded.
A speech to your supporters that night.

branches.then: The fireworks bought for it are never set off, and the empty lawn is the picture.
It is the record {winner}'s people read when you next need them.

sources.life: In his 2008 concession in Phoenix, some supporters booed when he said he had called Barack Obama, and at a mention of Joe Biden; applause rose when he praised the historic nature of Obama's win.

patterns.moment: In your concession speech, your supporters boo when you say {winner}'s name.
choices: quiet them and say the name again
let it pass and go on
patterns.ifNo: Letting it pass writes the speech as heard with the boos in it, a record {winner}'s people and the press read.

patterns.title: The night you lose the first round

roles.fill: the people who came to work for you

setting.text: Where the campaign gathered for the night.

gates: Candidate.
You lost the first round of a primary or caucus on the calendar.

branches.then: A microphone catches your voice and not the crowd's, and the yell at the end replays for days.
The next contest reads tonight.

sources.life: After finishing third in Iowa in 2004, he spoke to thousands of supporters and ended with a yell. A directional microphone cut out the crowd's noise, and the clip aired hundreds of times within days. He left the race in February.

patterns.moment: You finished far behind in the first contest, and the volunteers who came from everywhere wait for you to speak.
choices: rally them on to the next contest (a speech built one part at a time)
patterns.ifNo: Thanking them quietly writes the speech as heard, and some volunteers lapse on the campaign's record.

patterns.title: Your manager's boast

roles.fill: the manager who ran your race

setting.text: Where the story reaches you the next morning.

gates: You won.
{campaign manager}'s statement is on the press record.
weights: Whether the record holds any such payment.

branches.then: {campaign manager} recants under oath, calling it a story told to needle the other side. The lie is on their record.
Staff told groups the campaign would be ahead if they stayed out. It is on record and can be found.
Their leaders demand an apology and ask you to meet.

sources.person: Christine Todd Whitman and Ed Rollins
sources.life: Days after she won New Jersey's governorship in 1993, her campaign manager told reporters the campaign had paid to keep Black ministers and Democratic workers from turning out voters. He soon called it an exaggeration and later told lawyers under oath it was made up; Black ministers demanded an apology.

patterns.moment: Days after you won, {campaign manager} told reporters the campaign paid people not to turn out voters for {rival}.
choices: disown it and let them go
say it is false and keep them
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let it stand, and the groups it insulted ask why.

patterns.title: The bills after the race

roles.fill: the campaign's treasurer

setting.text: Where the campaign's books are kept.

gates: The campaign ended in debt on its reports.

branches.when: you take a post that bars you from raising money
branches.then: A relative or ally has to raise it for you.
They wait longest for their money, and they talk.

sources.life: She left the 2008 primary about $22.5 million in debt, millions of it her own loans, which she wrote off. As secretary of state she could not raise money herself, so Bill Clinton raised it; her pollster was paid last, and the debt was cleared in 2013.

patterns.moment: The race is over, the campaign owes vendors, staff and you, and {treasurer} asks who gets paid first.
choices: write off what you lent it
keep raising money to pay the vendors
rent the donor list to another campaign
patterns.ifNo: Letting the debt sit writes unpaid vendors who talk, and the reports show it each quarter.

patterns.title: Everyone wants the credit

roles.fill: the groups in your coalition on record: a union, a party faction, reformers, a neighborhood's organizers

setting.text: Wherever the calls reach you that morning.

gates: You won.
Backing from more than one group on record.
weights: How much each group's turnout mattered in the precinct results.

branches.then: Each side expects jobs, and giving to one costs the other.
Their organizers want a seat at the table.

sources.life: He won New York's mayoralty in 1933 with reform Democrats, Republicans, Socialists, and Jewish and most Italian voters, and once in office pushed Tammany appointees out.
In 1949 a coalition of newly registered Mexican American voters, Jewish voters and labor elected him to the Los Angeles council.

patterns.moment: The morning after you win, each group that backed you calls to say it won the race, and what it wants.
choices: ask each what it most needs
patterns.ifNo: Promising nothing writes no obligation. The groups wait, and the first to feel slighted says so.

patterns.title: Run again

roles.fill: your partner, a parent or your oldest friend

setting.text: Wherever you talk the next morning.

gates: You lost a race.
weights: How many times you have lost.

branches.then: The next try comes as a special election, and the papers call you the one who never quits.

branches.when: the incumbent who beat you retires
branches.then: The next run is against someone else.

sources.life: He lost three Wisconsin governor's races, then won the 1957 special Senate election.
He lost the 2002 Newark mayoral race and won in 2006, when the incumbent did not run.
She lost a 2012 state house race to the speaker, then won a Seattle council seat in 2013.

patterns.moment: You lost again, and {close tie} asks whether you will run next time.
choices: run again for the same office
patterns.ifNo: Saying you are done writes it, and the people who worked for you go elsewhere.

patterns.title: The oath

roles.fill: the person who gives the oath, said with the post
the book you swear on, or none

setting.text: where the oath is given, because the oath has its form.

gates: You won, and the oath is on the calendar.
weights: How unusual what you bring is in that body.

branches.then: You cannot raise the hand everyone is told to raise, so you raise the other, and the room goes quiet.
You ask for a book that means something to you. A member of the body tells voters he never would, and your answer is a record.

branches.when: a senior figure jokes about you
branches.then: Laugh, answer or let it pass. That figure later steers your committee.

sources.life: Sworn in as Hawaii's first representative in 1959 and asked to raise his right hand, he raised his left, having lost his right arm in the war. A colleague later said prejudice fell away in that moment.
The first Muslim in Congress took a ceremonial oath in 2007 on Thomas Jefferson's Quran, after a congressman wrote to voters criticizing the choice.
He was sworn in in 2009 on a Bible from the Wellstone family, and the oath was redone in the old chamber so his family could stand with him.

patterns.moment: {official} gives you the oath in its real form, and something about you is not the usual.
choices: which book, or an affirmation without one
a second ceremonial oath for your family
how to answer a critic of your choice
patterns.ifNo: Taking the plain form writes nothing extra, and a critic has nothing to say.

patterns.title: Nobody walks you in

roles.fill: the senior member from your state or place, with a grudge on record
a member from somewhere else

setting.text: the chamber floor, because the walk happens in front of everyone.

gates: You are being sworn in.
A custom of escort on record.
A grudge between you and {senior member} on record.

branches.when: the grudge goes back to a race
branches.then: You backed someone else against him once, and the record says why.
A tie, and a debt later votes read.

sources.life: When he came to take his Senate seat in 1875, Mississippi's senior senator, James Alcorn, refused to escort him and kept reading a newspaper. Roscoe Conkling of New York crossed the chamber and walked with him.

patterns.moment: Custom says {senior member} walks you to the oath, and he stays in his seat, reading.
choices: take {stranger}'s arm when he crosses the floor
patterns.ifNo: Walking alone writes nothing owed to anyone.

patterns.title: They will not seat you

roles.fill: a statement you made, a question about your citizenship or residence, or a complaint about how your election was run

setting.text: Where the vote happens, and where you hear it.

gates: You won.
A challenge to your seat on record.
weights: How many members are against you.

branches.then: The highest court rules unanimously that views cannot bar you, and you take the seat late.
Your papers were never finished, and {the body} votes you out.
You are one of several, and {the body} votes on all at once.

sources.life: In 1966 the Georgia House kept him out over his statements against the Vietnam War. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that a legislator's views cannot disqualify him, and he was seated.
In 1880 the California Senate voted to disqualify him after it came out that he had never completed his citizenship.
A New York congressman objected to seating Mississippi's members over the denial of Black voters' rights. The House seated them after a vote.

patterns.moment: {the body} votes not to seat you over {the challenge}.
choices: appear before the committee and explain
patterns.ifNo: Accepting writes the seat vacated, and another election or an appointment fills it.

patterns.title: Your first vote is the big one

roles.fill: the largest question on the record that week: a war, a bailout, an emergency

setting.text: the floor of {the body}, because the vote is cast there.

gates: First weeks in office.
A vote on {the question} on the calendar.

branches.then: The group that helped elect you says you set it back.
A member from elsewhere stands up for you, a tie.
Dozens of others vote with you.

sources.life: Four days after being sworn in as the first woman in Congress in 1917, she voted against entering World War I, speaking briefly as she voted, against House rules. The national suffrage group distanced itself; 49 other members also voted no.

patterns.moment: Days after your oath, {the body} votes on {the question}, and almost everyone is voting one way.
choices: vote no and say why, against the rules
patterns.ifNo: Voting with the majority writes the vote, and your cause's allies say nothing.

patterns.title: The vote that will not end

roles.fill: the member seeking to lead the body
a faction withholding its votes

setting.text: the floor of {the body}, because each round is cast there.

gates: The first day of a new term of {the body}.
The leadership vote has failed at least once.

branches.then: One member can now force a vote to remove the leader, and {holdouts} get seats on the rules committee.
Abstaining helps elect the leader without your name on it.

sources.life: It took 15 ballots over four days in January 2023 to elect him Speaker. No new member could be sworn in until it ended, and the holdouts won rule changes, including letting one member force a vote to remove the Speaker.

patterns.moment: The first act of {the body} is choosing its leader, the vote fails round after round, and no one is sworn in until it ends.
patterns.ifNo: Voting with the leadership writes a loyal vote, and {holdouts} win the rules without you.

patterns.title: Say nothing until you have something to say

roles.fill: the leader who picked you, or the chamber's senior figure

setting.text: Where {senior member} would take you aside.

gates: First term in a legislature.

branches.then: A member says the way to get along is to go along, and asks whether you will.
From high above the floor you learn who is who, a record of ties.

sources.life: Picked by Tammany leader Tom Foley for the New York Assembly, the young Smith got one piece of advice: do not speak until you have something to say. He sat as a back-bencher learning who was who.
The advice to get along by going along is tied to him, though no record of him saying it to new members is known.

patterns.moment: {senior member} tells you on your first day not to speak on the floor until you have something to say.
choices: follow it and learn the room
speak on your first bill anyway
ask what they want from you
patterns.ifNo: Following it writes a quiet first season, and colleagues learn your name slowly.

patterns.title: The chair who did not want you

roles.fill: the chair of the committee, said with years in the gavel
another member the chair opposed

setting.text: the committee's first meeting, because the slight is made in front of the members.

gates: You were put on a committee over its chair's objection.
{other newcomer} is on the same committee.

branches.when: the slight is one chair for two
branches.then: You and {other newcomer} share a single chair at the table, and the room sees it.

branches.when: {other newcomer} got the seat only because the leader stepped in
branches.then: You two are allies from here.
Reforms take the gavel away, and your silent protest is remembered.

sources.life: In 1973 Armed Services chairman F. Edward Hébert set out a single chair for the two newcomers he had opposed. They shared it as a silent protest, and Hébert lost his chairmanship in 1975.

patterns.moment: {committee chair}, who did not want you on the committee, slights you and {other newcomer} in front of everyone at the first meeting.
choices: take it together as a silent protest
patterns.ifNo: Standing by the wall writes nothing filed, and the chair has won the morning.

patterns.title: The first meeting is organized without you

roles.fill: the leader of the majority bloc against you

setting.text: {the body}'s first meeting, because the organizing vote is there.

gates: You are the new executive.
A majority of {the body} opposed you.

branches.then: The bloc names the chairs, and years of deadlock follow.

branches.when: a court or a special election changes the numbers
branches.then: The deadlock breaks.

sources.life: At his first Chicago council meeting in 1983, he and 21 allied aldermen walked out; the other 29 named the committee chairs, and the bloc blocked his appointments until special elections in 1986.

patterns.moment: At {the body}'s first meeting, {bloc leader}'s majority names the committee chairs without you.
choices: govern by veto and wait for the next election
patterns.ifNo: Staying silent writes that the bloc organized {the body} unopposed.

patterns.title: The hole in the budget

roles.fill: the official who runs the place's budget

setting.text: Wherever the executive works in the first week.

gates: An executive office in your first weeks.
A deficit on the budget record.

branches.then: The tax you said you would not raise is the only way left.
The people laid off are names in your place.
You push them out of the jobs they hold.

sources.life: Sworn in as California governor just after midnight in 1967, he found a shortfall, froze hiring and ordered cuts, then signed what was called the largest tax increase proposed by any governor.
Facing an inherited deficit in 1975, she laid off state workers and returned her own raise.
He inherited a deficit in 1934 and cut more than 1,000 positions in his first year.

patterns.moment: In your first week, {budget director} shows you the deficit you inherited.
choices: freeze hiring and cut every department
cut your own perks and pay first
patterns.ifNo: Putting it off writes nothing yet, and the hole grows on the record.

patterns.title: The promise on day one

roles.fill: the main pledge of your campaign on record

setting.text: Where the executive signs orders, on the first day.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the promise} is on record.

branches.then: You sign the order minutes after the oath. The cost lands on the budget and on the places that relied on the money.

branches.when: the police unit you ran against
branches.then: You disband it in your first weeks.
You veto budgets until the tax you promised against passes. Tens of thousands rally against you, and you may not run again.

sources.life: Minutes after his swearing-in as California governor in 2003, he signed an order repealing the tripled vehicle license fee, his main pledge.
After taking office as Detroit's mayor in 1974, he disbanded the police decoy unit he had campaigned against.

Elected in 1990 after saying he would not seek an income tax, he faced a large deficit, vetoed budgets without one, and signed a 6 percent income tax in 1991. Tens of thousands rallied against him, and he did not run again.

patterns.moment: {the promise} can be kept at once, by order, minutes after the oath, or broken when the numbers turn.
choices: keep it at once by order
patterns.ifNo: Delaying writes the promise as still open, and the people who voted for it count the days.

patterns.title: The order on the first day

roles.fill: a say members hold by custom over permits, licenses or jobs in their own districts

setting.text: Where the executive signs orders, on the first day.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the power} is on record.

branches.when: members are surprised at its reach
branches.then: They line up against your first bill.
Reformers say it is half done; members say you went too far.

sources.life: Right after her 2019 inauguration as Chicago mayor, she signed an order curbing aldermen's long-held say over permits and licenses in their wards, leaving zoning alone. Many aldermen were surprised at its reach.

patterns.moment: You can sign an order on your first day that takes a long-held power away from the members of {the body}.
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it alone writes that the custom stands, and the reformers who backed you ask why.

patterns.title: The perks you refuse

roles.fill: the office you now hold
your chief of staff

setting.text: Where the executive works in the first week.

gates: You hold an office with perks on record.

branches.when: a hole in the office rug
branches.then: You leave it, and members who come asking for favors see it.

branches.when: you live on part of your pay
branches.then: You give the rest away, a public pledge on your record.

sources.life: As California's new governor in 1975, he refused the new governor's residence, rented an apartment, and drove a Plymouth instead of riding in a limousine.
She returned a $7,000 raise and sold the state's limousine and plane.
After winning her council seat she said she would live on about $40,000 of her salary.

patterns.moment: The residence, the car and the raise come with {the office}, and {chief of staff} asks which you will take.
patterns.ifNo: Taking it all writes nothing, and the press may count it.

patterns.title: Who gets the work

roles.fill: a large public project on record
firms owned by people the old contracts shut out

setting.text: Wherever the executive meets the builders.

gates: You hold an executive office.
{the project} is on record with contracts {the left out} had no part in.

branches.when: business and state leaders push back
branches.then: Lawsuits threaten, and the work sits idle.

branches.when: the work resumes with a share
branches.then: Years later, the share of work those firms did is the record.

sources.life: In 1975 Atlanta's mayor halted work and withheld payment on the airport expansion to bring minority firms into its contracts. Despite pushback from business and state leaders, work resumed with a required minority share, and by 1980 minority firms did about a quarter of the work.

patterns.moment: {the project} was contracted before you took office, and almost none of the work goes to {the left out}.
choices: stop the work until the contracts are redone
set a share for new contracts only
let it go ahead and fight later
patterns.ifNo: Letting it go ahead writes the contracts as they were, and the people who elected you count it.

patterns.title: The strike on day one

roles.fill: a public workers' union on record
its leader, said with years at its head

setting.text: Wherever the talks are held.

gates: You take office.
A public contract on record that runs out that day, or a strike on the record.

branches.then: A judge orders {the union}'s leaders arrested, and the strike hardens.
Wages rise, and the state passes a law limiting public strikes.
The press says you talked down to them instead of bargaining.

sources.life: New York's transit workers struck on his first day as mayor in 1966. Their leader, Mike Quill, was jailed; after twelve days the union took a mediators' package, and the state later passed a law restricting public-employee strikes.

patterns.moment: The contract with {the union} runs out the day you take office, and the workers walk out.
choices: ask a judge to enforce the law
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes nothing, and the place stops running.

patterns.title: The storm that decides the next race

roles.fill: whoever means to run against you
a storm, flood, fire, heat wave or outage on the world's record

setting.text: Wherever the response is run from, or out with the crews.

gates: You hold the executive office.
{the disaster} is on the record in your place.

branches.then: The plows fall behind, trains stop on some lines, and the snow sits for weeks.
The response is your campaign.
Those voters remember it at the primary.

sources.life: A January 1979 blizzard paralyzed Chicago and the plows fell behind. Byrne used the anger to beat the sitting mayor, Bilandic, in the primary weeks later.

patterns.moment: The first disaster of your term, {the disaster}, hits {the place}, the response falls behind, and {challenger} is watching.
choices: say the place is handling it
open the books on the response
patterns.ifNo: Saying it is handled writes your words against the record of the streets.
